## Methods

### Animals and sample collection

Two adult sea cucumbers were collected from the northeastern rocky region of Puerto Rico and were kept in aerated sea water for acclimatization prior to experiments. Evisceration of the sea cucumber was stimulated by intracoelomic injection of 0.35 M KCl as previously described (Reyes-Rivera et al., 2024). They were maintained in sea water aquaria for 9 days to undergo regeneration until dissection. Before the dissection, animals were anesthetized by immersion in ice-cold water for 45 minutes. Dissection was done through an initial dorsal incision which allowed exposition of the internal organs, upon which the growing anlage (or rudiment) and mesentery were dissected and separated from each other. Each tissue was kept in CMFSS on ice and treated separately during the tissue dissociation process. Thus, tissues were dissected for four scRNA-seqs; two anlage samples and two mesentery samples.

### Tissue dissociation

Mesentery and anlage tissues were digested for 15 minutes, in rocking shaker at room temperature with 1 mL of 0.05% Trypsin/0.02% EDTA solution prepared in Ca++ and Mg++ free sea water (CMFSS) (Bello et al., 2015). Digestions were quenched by adding 500 µL of 0.2% bovine serum albumen (BSA) in CMFSS and then centrifuged for 2 minutes at 1500 rpm. The supernatants were discarded, the pellets resuspended with 500 µL of 0.04% BSA in CMFSS, and the cells were gently separated by pipetting using glass pipettes with fire-blunted tips. The cell suspensions were filtered using a nylon cell strainer with 70 mm mesh, and aliquots were taken for cell counting. Cell viability was assessed through manual cell counting with hemocytometer to confirm that a viability higher than 90% was maintained. Sample suspensions were adjusted to 1000 cells/mL using CMFSS as required for sequencing procedures.

### Immuno- and cytochemistry

50 µL of dissociated cell sample (from the same samples that were used for scRNAseq) were placed on polysine-treated slides and fixed with 50 µL of 4% paraformaldehyde and left to dry overnight. Slides were washed in phosphate buffered saline (PBS) prior to use for immune and or cytochemistry. The methodology for the immunofluorescence techniques/preparation of slides was followed as published except for the time of PBS washes, which were of 10 minutes instead of 15 minutes (Díaz-Balzac et al., 2007; Reyes-Rivera et al., 2024). The primary and secondary antibodies used are in Figure 1—source data 1. Samples to be probed with fluorescent phalloidin were treated directly with Phalloidin-TRITC (1:1000; Sigma P1951) for 1 hr as described previously (Reyes-Rivera et al., 2024). DAPI was incorporated into the mounting medium as described previously (Reyes-Rivera et al., 2024). Cells were observed in a Nikon DS-Qi2 fluorescent microscope.

### Single-cell RNA sequencing and data analysis

Single-cell libraries were prepared using the 10X Genomics Chromium Next GEM Single Cell 3' Kit v3.1 and the Chromium 10X instrument, following the protocol from manufacturer (CG000204). Sequencing was carried out with Illumina NextSeq 2000 at the Sequencing and Genotyping Facility of the University of Puerto Rico Molecular Science Building.

The raw sequencing reads from all four samples (two mesentery and two anlage) were processed individually using Cell Ranger (v7.1.0) (Zheng et al., 2017) using the reference genome and gene models of H. glaberrima available at http://blastkit.hpcf.upr.edu/hglaberrima-v1. Gene models were annotated against human reference proteins from UniProt and the entire UniProt reference protein database. Gene IDs throughout the study correspond to the annotations with the human reference protein sequences from UnitProt.

Samples quality was assessed through the number of UMI, genes, and overall complexity of gene expression. The number of UMI and genes was found to be over 500 and 300, respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 1). Furthermore, the distribution of genes per cells was found to be unimodal. In general aspects, samples from each animal were similar, with the total number of cells from the anlage tissue higher than that of the mesentery. General sequencing statistics after mapping reads with Cell Ranger can be found in Figure 2—source data 1.

Initial quality filtering was conducted in R (v4.3.2) using SoupX (v1.6.2) with default parameters to remove ambient RNA (Young and Behjati, 2020). Subsequent data processing was carried out using Seurat (v4.3.0.1) (Hao et al., 2024; Hao et al., 2021; Satija et al., 2015; Stuart et al., 2019). After data normalization and identifying variable features (n=2000), 22,970 anchors were identified using 20 dimensions. The datasets were integrated using the canonical correlation analysis approach of Seurat, followed by data scaling for principal component analysis (npcs = 50) and Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) dimensional reduction technique (dims = 1:20).

Neighbors were then identified with 20 dimensions, leading to cluster identification at a resolution of 0.5. Various resolution parameters (0.8, 1.2, and 1.4) and dimensions (up to 35 in increments of 5) were tested before the final resolution value. The statistical analysis tool scSHC was employed to assess the probability of each cluster being unique (Grabski et al., 2023). Marker genes of each cluster or supra-clusters were identified using the FindMarkers() function in Seurat and mapped to the appropriate UniProt IDs. Genes highlighted throughout the study were further validated using the NCBI non-redundant reference database and EchinoBase (Telmer et al., 2024) via BLAST.

Differential expression data across clusters was used to perform gene set enrichment analysis of Gene Ontology (gseGO) biological processes terms using clusterProfiler (v.10.0) (Yu et al., 2012) with a p-value cutoff of 0.05. For this analysis, BLASTp was used to map H. glaberrima gene models to human reference protein sequences from NCBI (GCF_000001405.40), facilitating the assignment of ENTREZ ID to the correct human GO terms in the AnnotationDbi (v1.64.1) human database (v2.1) (Pagès et al., 2024).

RNA velocity loom files were generated with velocyto (v0.17), which relied on genome-masked regions obtained from RepeatModeler (v2.0.5) and RepeatMasker (v4.1.5) (Smit et al., 2015; Smit and Hubley, 2015), along with the sea cucumber gene models and CellRanger dataset. These files were further analyzed with velocyto.R (v0.6) and SeuratWrappers (v0.2.0), using the ReadVelocity and RunVelocity functions. Pseudotime analysis for the distinct data subsets was conducted using Slingshot (v2.10.0) (Street et al., 2018). The code of the data analysis has been made available at GitHub (copy archived at Medina, 2024).

### HCR-FISH

Regenerating intestines from animals eviscerated 8–9 days previously and intestines from non-eviscerated (controls) animals were collected and fixed in 4% (v/v) paraformaldehyde with phosphate-buffered saline (0.01 M PBS; 0.138 M NaCl; 0.0027 M KCl; pH7.4) overnight at 4℃. Tissues were then washed three times by PBS and treated overnight with 40% saccharose prior to cutting in the cryostat. Sections (20 mm) were prepared in a cryostat (Leica CM1850), as previously published for immunohistochemistry (Reyes-Rivera et al., 2024). Gene spatial expression was determined by designing 12 or 24 set split probes for each gene marker. To decrease probe unspecific binding and increase its signal to background ratio, probes were designed as described by H. Choi and colleagues (Molecular Instruments) (Choi et al., 2018). To ensure probe gene target specificity, all nucleotide regions selected for probe design underwent extensive validation using the newly developed H. glaberrima genome and transcriptome alignment tool (https://blastkit.hpcf.upr.edu/hglaberrima-v1/; Medina-Feliciano et al., 2021). Probes were used at a final concentration of approximately 20–25 nM.

Immediately after slide preparation, HCR-FISH v3 was carried out using a modified version of Molecular Instrument’s fresh fixed frozen tissues protocol. Probe hybridization was conducted overnight at 37℃, while DNA hairpin amplification (B1-546nm or B2-546nm) was done at 25℃ overnight with 3 pmol of h1 and h2, respectively. Our protocol modification involved replacing ethanol with methanol during sample permeabilization. Also, the use of proteinase K was omitted, and Tween 20 at 0.1% was added to all PBS wash buffers. Once slides were prepared, image acquisition was attained using a Nikon DS-Qi2 fluorescent microscope. Positive control probes (PolyA) were used as signal calibrators to define background from positive signal during image analysis (Figure 4—figure supplement 2). Negative controls with fluorescent hairpins only can be found in Figure 7—figure supplement 1. Each probe was studied in at least three different animals, none of which were the specimens used for the scRNA-seq.

Summary:

Joshua G. Medina-Feliciano et al. investigated the single-cell transcriptomic profile of holoturian regenerating intestine following evisceration, a process used to expel their viscera in response to predation. Using single-cell RNA-Sequencing and standard analysis such as "Find cluster markers", "Enrichment analysis of Gene Ontology" and "RNA velocity", they identify 13 cell clusters and their potential cell identity. Based on bioinformatic analysis they identified potentially proliferating clusters and potential trajectories of cell differentiation. This manuscript represents a useful dataset that can provide candidate cell types and cell markers for more in-depth functional analysis of the holoturian intestine regeneration.

The conclusions of this paper are supported only by bioinformatic analyses since the in vivo validation through HCR is not sufficient to support them.

Strengths:

- The Authors are providing a single-cell dataset obtained from sea cucumbers regenerating their intestines. This represents the first fundamental step to an unbiased approach to better understand this regeneration process and the cellular dynamics taking part in it.

- The Authors run all the standard analyses providing the reader with a well digested set of information about cell clusters, potential cell types, potential functions and potential cell differentiation trajectories.

Weaknesses:

- The Authors frequently report the percentage of cells with a specific feature (either labelled or expressing a certain gene or belonging to a certain cluster). This number can be misleading since that is calculated after cell dissociation and additional procedures (such as staining or sequencing and dataset cleanup) that can heavily bias the ratio between cell types. Similarly, the Authors cannot compare cell percentage between anlage and mesentery samples since that can be affected by technical aspects related to cell dissociation, tissue composition and sequencing depth.

- The Authors did not validate all the clusters.

- There is no validation of the trajectory analysis and there is no validation of the proliferating cluster with H3P or EdU co-labeling.

## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.100796.3.sa3](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.100796.3.sa3)

Summary:

The authors have done a good job at creating a "resource" paper for the study of gut regeneration in sea cucumbers. They present a single-cell RNAseq atlas for the reconstitution of Holothuria glaberrima gut following self-evisceration in response to a potassium chloride injection. The authors provide data characterizing cellular populations and precursors of the regenerating anlage at 9 days post evisceration. As a "Tools and Resources" contribution to eLife, this work, with some revisions, could be appropriate. It will be impactful in the fields of regeneration, particularly in invertebrates, but also in comparative studies in other species, including evolutionary studies. Some of these comparative studies could extend to vertebrates and could therefore impact regenerative medicine in the future.

Strengths:

• Novel and useful information for a model organism and question for which this type of data has not yet been reported

• Single-cell gene expression data will be valuable for developing testable hypotheses in the future

• Marker genes for cell types provided to the field

• Interesting predictions about possible lineage relationships between cells during sea cucumber gut regeneration

• Authors have done a good job in the revision of making sure not to overstate the lineage claims in absence of definitive lineage-tracing experiments

• Authors have improved the figures and the overall readability of the figures and text

Specific questions:

- Is there any way to systematically compare these cells to evolutionarily-diverged cells in distant relatives to sea cucumbers? Or even on a case-by-case basis? For example, is there evidence for any of these transitory cell types to have correlate(s) in vertebrate gut regeneration?

• Authors acknowledged this would be interesting and important, but they say in the response document this is outside the scope of the current manuscript and more data would be needed to do this well.

- Line 808: The authors may make a more accurate conclusion by saying that the characteristics are similar to blastemas or behaves like a blastema rather than it is blastema. There is ambiguity about the meaning of this term in the field, but most researchers seem to currently have in mind that the "blastema" definitions includes a discrete spatial organization of cells, and here these cells are much more spread out. This could be a good opportunity for the authors to engage in this dialogue, perhaps parsing out the nuances of what a "blastema" is, what the term has traditionally referred to, and how we might consider updating this term or at least re-framing the terminology to be inclusive of functions that "blastemas" have traditionally had in the literature and how they may be dispersed over geographical space in an organism more so than the more rigid, geographically-restricted definition many researchers have in mind. However, if the authors choose to elaborate on these issues, those elaborations do belong in the discussion, and the more provisional terminology we mention here could be used throughout the paper until that element of the revised discussion is presented. We would welcome the authors to do this as a way to point the field in this direction as this is also how we view the matter. For example, some of the genes whose expression has been observed to be enriched following removal of brain tissue in axolotls (such as kazald2, Lust et al.), are also upregulated in traditional blastemas, for instance, in the limb, but we appreciate that the expression domain may not be as localized as in a limb blastema. Additionally, since there is now evidence that some aspects of progenitor cell activation even in limb regeneration extend far beyond the local site of amputation injury (Johnson et al., Payzin-Dogru et al.), there is an opportunity to connect the dots and make the claim that there could be more dispersion of "blastema function" than previously appreciated in the field. Diving a bit more into these nuances may also enable a better conceptual framework of how blastema function may evolve across vast evolutionary time and between different injury contexts in super-regenerative organisms.

• Authors addressed this comment and agree it is interesting, but given how much territory they had to cover and space limitations, they will save this type of discussion and comparative theoretical work for the future.

Overall, the manuscript is much improved.

claims.claim: The intestinal anlage is a particular regenerative structure that has long been described as a blastema-like structure due to its morphological resemblance to the 'classical blastema'.
claims.source: The intestinal anlage is a particular regenerative structure that has long been described as a blastema-like structure due to its remarkable morphological resemblance to the 'classical blastema' (García-Arrarás, 1998).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: A blastema is usually described as a transient structure composed of a mass of proliferating undifferentiated cells found at the site of injury that will give rise to the regenerated organ.
claims.source: As stated previously, a blastema is usually described as a transient structure composed of a mass of proliferating undifferentiated cells. This structure is found at the site of injury and will give rise to the regenerated organ (Seifert and Muneoka, 2018).
claims.evidence: This is a general definition of a blastema supported by citation.

claims.claim: The blastema cells can originate from different lineages across species.
claims.source: The blastema cells can originate from different lineages across species. For example, in some amphibians the blastemal cells originate from dedifferentiated muscle, cartilage, fibroblast, and other tissues, while in others they include cells that originate from muscle satellite cells, a type of stem cell (Globus et al., 1980; Sandoval-Guzmán et al., 2014). In Planaria, they originate from undifferentiated stem cells known as neoblasts (Baguñà, 2012; Wagner et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to studies in various organisms.

claims.claim: The blastema is overlayed by a wound epidermis that develops into a specialized wound epidermis known as the apical epithelial cap (AEC) in amphibians.
claims.source: The blastema is overlayed by a wound epidermis that is formed by a re-epithelization process following injury, which develops into a specialized wound epidermis that in amphibians is known as the apical epithelial cap (AEC) (Aztekin, 2021).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation.

claims.claim: The presence or absence of a blastema defines the regenerative success or failure of the regeneration process.
claims.source: Since its first description, more than 100 years ago, the blastema has been regarded as the best indicator of regeneration, and its presence is associated with tissues or organs that are highly regenerative. In fact, it has been proposed that the presence or absence of a blastema defines the regenerative success or failure of the regeneration process.
claims.evidence: This is a general statement about the role of the blastema in regeneration.

claims.claim: The classical definition of a blastema has been reconsidered, moving toward its functional role rather than its histological or structural characteristics.
claims.source: However, as more regenerative species continue to be studied, the classical definition of a blastema has been reconsidered, moving toward its functional role rather than its histological or structural characteristics (Seifert and Muneoka, 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation.

claims.claim: The sea cucumber intestinal anlage stands as a different structure in terms of the tissue compartmentalization of certain activities compared to the amphibian blastema.
claims.source: The sea cucumber intestinal anlage stands as a different structure in terms of the tissue compartmentalization of certain activities.
claims.evidence: This is a comparison based on the findings of the study.

claims.claim: Similar to some amphibian blastema cells, the cells of the holothurian anlage coelomic epithelium are proliferative undifferentiated cells that originated via a dedifferentiation process.
claims.source: For instance, we and others have previously described the dedifferentiation process by which muscle cells dedifferentiate and proliferate (García-Arrarás et al., 2011; Dolmatov, 2021). Thus, similar to some amphibian blastema cells, the cells of the holothurian anlage coelomic epithelium are proliferative undifferentiated cells that originated via a dedifferentiation process.
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison with amphibian blastema and supported by citations.

claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on sea cucumber regeneration.

claims.source: In amphibians, some of these factors are thought to be released by cells of the AEC, serving as a way of modulating the blastema cell activity. For example, FGF1 is expressed in the cells of the AEC while FGF receptors were localized to blastema cells (Zenjari et al., 1996).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to a study on amphibian regeneration.

claims.claim: Both FGF and Wnt signaling have been shown to be vital for the formation of the blastema in amphibians.
claims.source: Moreover, both FGF and Wnt signaling have been shown to be vital for the formation of the blastema (Makanae et al., 2014).

claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent study.

claims.source: Similar results have been shown for Wnt, primarily a study by our laboratory demonstrating that Wnt pathway inhibition, either by pharmacological drugs or by RNAi, caused a reduction in cell proliferation (Alicea-Delgado and García-Arrarás, 2021; Bello et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to studies by the authors' laboratory.

claims.claim: In the sea cucumber coelomic epithelium of the anlage, cells are involved in intercellular communications that modulate cellular dynamics through factors similar to those found in the AEC-blastema cell modulation.
claims.source: Thus, in the sea cucumber coelomic epithelium of the anlage, cells are also involved in intercellular communications that modulate cellular dynamics through factors similar to those found in the AEC-blastema cell modulation.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on comparison with amphibian regeneration.

claims.claim: Both PRRX1, a gene expressed by amphibian blastema cell precursors, and HES1, a marker gene of the amphibian AEC, are expressed by the holothurian coelomic epithelium.
claims.source: In fact, both PRRX1 (paired mesoderm homeobox protein), a gene expressed by amphibian blastema cell precursors (Gerber et al., 2018; Lin et al., 2021), and HES1 (transcription factor HES-1), a marker gene of the amphibian AEC, are expressed by the holothurian coelomic epithelium (Aztekin, 2021; Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This is based on gene expression analysis and comparison with amphibian studies.

results.result: The study employed scRNA-seq and HCR-FISH to identify 13 distinct cell clusters in the 9-day post-evisceration regenerating intestinal anlage and mesentery of Holothuria glaberrima, with 3844 total cells analyzed (2392 from anlage, 1452 from mesentery).
results.evaluation: The methodological approach is clearly described (C3, C36, C37, C41), the timepoint selection is justified (C38), and the primary quantitative results are reported (C4, C55, C56). The clustering analysis is supported by appropriate statistical validation (C59) and quality control metrics are provided. The experimental design of separating anlage from mesentery tissues is sound.

results.result: The 13 clusters segregate into two major supra-clusters representing coelomic epithelial cells (7 clusters, 69.6% of cells) and mesenchymal cells (2 clusters, 19.1% of cells), with 4 additional clusters representing coelomocyte populations (11.3% of cells).
results.evaluation: The characterization is based on differential gene expression analysis (C60, C61, C67, C69) with appropriate marker genes (ERG for mesenchymal, WNT9 for epithelial) validated by prior in situ studies (C68, C70). The quantitative distribution across clusters is clearly reported (C63-C65) and the immune-related gene expression supports coelomocyte identification (C73, C80). HCR-FISH validation strengthens the conclusions (C83-C85).

results.result: Four distinct coelomocyte/immune cell populations (C6, C10, C11, C12) were identified based on immune-related gene expression, with C6 uniquely expressing FBCD1 and C12 expressing BAR3, validated by HCR-FISH showing widespread distribution in tissues.
results.evaluation: The identification is based on differential expression of immune-related genes (C79, C80, C81, C82) with GO enrichment supporting immune functions (C80). HCR-FISH validation confirms distinct cell types with appropriate tissue distribution (C83-C85). The claim of being the first expression profile of coelomocyte populations in adult echinoderms (C154) is appropriately qualified. However, the exact correspondence to previously described morphological types (C153) remains to be established.

results.result: Two mesenchymal cell populations (C2 and C7) were identified expressing ECM-related genes (TIMP3, HMCN1, MMP14, ERG), with C2 representing recently EMT-transitioned cells and C7 representing more differentiated mesenchymal cells, validated by HMCN1 HCR-FISH.
results.evaluation: The characterization is based on expression of multiple ECM-related genes (C89-C91) with support from studies in other echinoderms (C148-C149). The developmental relationship between C2 and C7 is supported by pseudotime analysis (C92, C151). HCR-FISH validation shows appropriate spatial distribution (C93-C95). However, the EMT hypothesis (C92) requires additional validation beyond gene expression and pseudotime analysis.

results.result: Cluster C8 represents proliferating cells expressing markers PLK1, PCNA, CDK1, KI67, and TOP2A, with higher representation in anlage (4%) than mesentery (2%), validated by KI67 HCR-FISH and BrdU labeling in the coelomic epithelium.
results.evaluation: The proliferative identity is strongly supported by expression of multiple established proliferation markers (C98, C99) and validated by both HCR-FISH (C101) and BrdU labeling (C102). The differential distribution between anlage and mesentery (C100) is consistent with prior observations (C155). However, the exact role of C8 in the differentiation hierarchy (C156, C157) remains somewhat uncertain and requires additional lineage tracing experiments.

results.result: Cluster C5 represents muscle precursor cells expressing TITIN, MYL1, MYH7, ACTG, and CNN3, localized to the basal region of the coelomic epithelium, validated by MYH7 HCR-FISH and co-expression with muscle-specific antibody.
results.evaluation: The muscle precursor identity is strongly supported by expression of multiple muscle-specific markers (C104) and validated by HCR-FISH showing appropriate spatial localization (C105, C106). Double labeling experiments confirm cells are forming contractile apparatus (C107). The characterization is consistent with prior studies (C103, C158) and comparative data from other species (C159).

results.result: Cluster C9 represents neuroepithelial cells expressing neuronal genes (NETR, PRD10, ELAV2, STA10/STARD10), validated by STA10 HCR-FISH and double labeling with RN1 antibody showing fiber extensions typical of differentiating neurons.
results.evaluation: The neuroepithelial identity is supported by expression of multiple neuronal markers (C109) with validation by HCR-FISH (C111) and double labeling showing both mRNA and protein expression (C112). The characterization is consistent with prior studies (C110, C161) and comparative data from other organisms (C160). The cells represent differentiating rather than fully mature neurons.

results.result: Cluster C4 represents differentiating coelomic epithelial cells expressing KCNQ5, SC6A9, EFNB2, and UNC5C, with cells predominantly from mesentery (67%) rather than anlage (37%), validated by UNC5C HCR-FISH showing expression in normal intestine mesothelium and regenerating mesentery.
results.evaluation: The characterization is based on differential gene expression (C113) with GO enrichment supporting advanced developmental stages (C114). The tissue distribution is clearly quantified (C115). HCR-FISH validation shows appropriate spatial pattern (C116, C117) supporting the interpretation that these cells are differentiating toward coelomic epithelium of the regenerated organ (C118). However, the exact identity requires further validation.

results.result: Clusters C0, C1, and C3 represent coelomic epithelial cells at different differentiation stages, with C1 and C3 predominantly in anlage (37% of anlage cells) expressing developmental genes and pluripotency markers (PIWL1, YAP1, HES1, HSP90A), while C0 is more associated with mesentery (27% of mesentery cells), validated by NET1 and TRFM HCR-FISH showing distinct spatial patterns.
results.evaluation: The characterization is based on shared gene expression (C119, C120) with distinct spatial distributions (C121-C123). HCR-FISH validation shows clear differential expression patterns (C124-C127) supporting distinct identities (C128). The expression of pluripotency markers (C167-C169) with support from comparative studies (C170) strengthens the precursor cell hypothesis. Trajectory analysis supports developmental relationships (C164, C171). However, definitive proof of pluripotency requires lineage tracing experiments.

results.result: The coelomic epithelium of the anlage is pluripotent, with cells from C1 and C3 serving as precursor populations that can differentiate into muscle (C5), neurons (C9), coelomic epithelia (C4), and mesenchymal cells (C2/C7), supported by trajectory analysis and expression of pluripotency markers.
results.evaluation: While the identification of multiple differentiation pathways from epithelial precursors is well-supported by trajectory analysis (C134-C142, C164, C171) and gene expression (C166-C169), the claim of pluripotency (C10, C173) is not definitively proven. The evidence is consistent with pluripotency but lacks direct lineage tracing experiments. Support from other echinoderm species (C174-C177) is suggestive but not conclusive. The hypothesis is reasonable but requires additional experimental validation.

results.result: RNA velocity and Slingshot pseudotime analyses show that C5, C9, and C4 are terminal differentiation states, C8 (proliferating cells) transitions into C1, and C1 represents the least differentiated precursor state that gives rise to C3 and C4, with C0 representing a more advanced differentiation state.
results.evaluation: The trajectory analysis is based on appropriate computational methods (RNA velocity and Slingshot) with consistent results across different analytical approaches (C134-C142). The interpretation is supported by the biological context and gene expression patterns. However, RNA velocity analysis has inherent limitations and assumptions that should be acknowledged. The conclusions would be strengthened by experimental validation through lineage tracing.

results.result: The sea cucumber intestinal anlage functions as a blastema-like structure, with the coelomic epithelium cells serving as blastemal cells that express similar signaling factors (Wnt, FGF, TGF-beta) to amphibian blastema/AEC, but differs in that cells with both blastema and AEC characteristics are found within the same epithelial layer rather than being spatially separated.
results.evaluation: The comparison to amphibian blastema is well-supported by expression of similar signaling molecules (C190, C193-C195) and functional similarities (C189, C200). The key difference in tissue organization (C197-C199) is clearly articulated. However, this is primarily a conceptual/comparative analysis rather than direct experimental demonstration. The functional equivalence is inferred from gene expression and prior functional studies rather than demonstrated de novo.

results.result: The holothurian intestinal regeneration process involves formation of an anlage at the injured mesentery tip through dedifferentiation and proliferation of coelomic epithelial cells, which differs from classical blastemas in that proliferation occurs mainly in the epithelium rather than mesenchyme.
results.evaluation: This is a summary of established knowledge about holothurian regeneration supported by multiple prior studies (C17-C20, C27-C32). The temporal sequence is documented (C21-C24) and the key distinction from classical blastemas is clearly stated (C20). This provides essential context for interpreting the scRNA-seq results but represents prior work rather than new findings from this study.

results.result: Immunocytochemical analysis of dissociated cells showed that the sequenced populations correspond to previously described cell types, with most cells (32-60%) expressing mesothelial markers, 40% mesenchymal markers, 5% immune cell markers, and 2-7% muscle markers, though mature muscle cells and neurons were not dissociated by the protocol.
results.evaluation: The immunocytochemical characterization provides important validation that the dissociated cells represent expected populations (C42-C47, C54). The quantification is clear and the limitations of the dissociation protocol are appropriately acknowledged (C52, C53). This quality control analysis strengthens confidence in the scRNA-seq results but represents a methodological validation rather than a primary finding.

results.result: The 13 identified clusters show varying sizes (21% to 1% of total cells), each contains cells from both anlage and mesentery samples, and most clusters (except C3 and C4) were statistically validated by scSHC analysis, with each cluster exhibiting distinctive gene expression profiles.
results.evaluation: The quantitative characterization of cluster properties is clearly reported (C57, C58, C60, C61) with appropriate statistical validation (C59). The acknowledgment that C3 and C4 were not validated by scSHC is appropriate, though their uniqueness is supported by other analyses. This represents standard quality control and characterization of clustering results.

results.result: This is the first application of scRNA-seq and HCR-FISH to adult echinoderm regeneration, focusing on 9-dpe regenerating intestine where cells are undergoing dedifferentiation and differentiation, with the unexpected finding that anlage and mesentery show similar cell cluster composition explained by gradient processes and protocol limitations.
results.evaluation: The novelty claim (C143) is appropriately qualified and the study focus is clearly stated (C144). The unexpected finding of similar clusters between tissues (C145) is thoughtfully explained by biological gradients (C146) and technical limitations (C147). This represents appropriate contextualization of the study's scope and limitations.

results.result: Animals show diverse regenerative capacities across species and tissues, with echinoderms being prime examples among deuterostomes, and scRNA-seq has been successfully applied to study regeneration in various model organisms including mammals, axolotl, planaria, and echinoderm embryos.
results.evaluation: These claims represent well-established background knowledge in regenerative biology (C11-C16) and prior applications of scRNA-seq (C35), all appropriately supported by citations. This provides necessary context but does not represent findings from the current study.

results.result: Coelomocytes are specialized immune cells found in echinoderm coelomic fluid and organs with roles in pathogen recognition, phagocytosis, and other immune functions, and have been shown to be present in holothurian injury sites, mesentery, and regeneration anlage.
results.evaluation: These claims represent established knowledge about coelomocyte biology (C75, C76) and their presence in regenerating tissues (C77), appropriately supported by citations. This provides necessary background for interpreting the coelomocyte clusters identified in the study.

results.result: The coelomic epithelium of regenerating tissues differs morphologically and molecularly from normal mesothelium, is composed of dedifferentiated cells, and is responsible for most cell division in the regenerating intestine.
results.evaluation: These claims represent established knowledge from prior studies (C96, C97) appropriately supported by citations. This provides essential context for understanding the coelomic epithelial clusters identified in the scRNA-seq analysis.

results.result: The mesentery coelomic epithelium (C0) expresses SAA1, an immune-related gene, raising the possibility that the coelomic epithelium could be a source of coelomocytes, as observed in other echinoderms.
results.evaluation: The observation of SAA1 expression in C0 is data-supported (C178) and consistent with prior localization studies (C179). The hypothesis that coelomic epithelium could generate coelomocytes is supported by observations in other echinoderms (C180) but remains speculative for this system. The authors appropriately present this as a possibility rather than a conclusion, but it requires experimental validation.

results.result: The normal intestine consists of three layers (mesothelium including coelomic epithelium and muscle, connective tissue, and luminal epithelium) that are continuous with the mesentery and body wall, and at 9 dpe the anlage consists of epithelial cells surrounding connective tissue with mesenchymal cells.
results.evaluation: These are straightforward anatomical descriptions (C25, C26, C39) supported by the figures and consistent with established holothurian anatomy. This provides necessary structural context for interpreting the cellular analysis.

results.result: The authors employed scRNA-seq and HCR-FISH to analyze the regenerating intestinal anlage of Holothuria glaberrima at 9 days post-evisceration, representing the first use of these techniques in adult echinoderms to study regeneration. The anlage was separated from the mesentery and both tissues were processed independently for scRNA-seq.
results.evaluation: All reviewers acknowledge this as a novel and valuable methodological contribution. Reviewers explicitly state this is 'the first fundamental step to an unbiased approach' and 'novel and useful information for a model organism.' The editor notes the manuscript 'provides some new findings about organ regeneration' using these state-of-the-art techniques.

results.result: The scRNA-seq analysis identified 13 distinct cell clusters in the regenerating anlage, with each cluster exhibiting distinctive gene expression profiles. The clusters ranged from 21% (cluster 0) to 1% (cluster 12) of total cells, and each cluster contained cells from both mesentery and anlage samples. Most clusters were supported by statistical significance analysis (scSHC), except C3 and C4.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the identification of 13 clusters as a primary finding. One reviewer notes 'The Authors run all the standard analyses providing the reader with a well digested set of information about cell clusters.' However, one reviewer notes 'The Authors did not validate all the clusters,' indicating some uncertainty about complete validation.

results.result: The 13 clusters segregated into distinct groups: two clusters (C2, C7) representing mesenchymal cells expressing ERG, seven clusters representing coelomic epithelial cells expressing WNT9, and four clusters representing coelomocyte/immune cell populations. About 90% of cells segregated into two main supra-clusters corresponding to coelomic epithelial and mesenchymal cell types.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this broad characterization of cell types. The editor notes the work 'provides some new findings about organ regeneration, as well as the origins of pluripotent cells.' One reviewer acknowledges the authors 'identify 13 cell clusters and their potential cell identity' based on standard bioinformatic analyses.

results.result: Four clusters (C6, C10, C11, C12) were identified as coelomocyte/immune cell populations based on immune-related gene expression. C6 expressed FBCD1 and showed GO enrichment for immune responses. HCR-FISH validation showed FBCD1 and BAR3-expressing cells were heterogeneously distributed throughout tissues. This represents the first expression profile report of distinct coelomocyte populations in an adult echinoderm.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the identification of immune cell populations. The HCR-FISH validation is noted as 'convincing RNA localization images' by the editor. However, one reviewer notes 'The Authors did not validate all the clusters,' suggesting not all immune clusters received equal validation.

results.result: Two mesenchymal clusters (C2 and C7) were identified, with C2 expressing ECM-related genes (TIMP3, HMCN1, MMP14, MMP24) and proposed to represent cells recently undergoing EMT, while C7 represents more specialized mesenchymal cells. HCR-FISH for HMCN1 showed differential labeling patterns supporting this interpretation.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the mesenchymal cell characterization. The HCR-FISH validation is acknowledged as providing spatial context. However, the interpretation of C2 as recently EMT-derived cells is based on inference from gene expression and pseudotime analysis, which one reviewer notes is 'supported only by bioinformatic analyses.'

results.result: C8 represents proliferating cells expressing markers such as PLK1, SMC2, PCNA, CDK1, and TOP2A, primarily localized within the anlage coelomic epithelium (4% in anlage vs 2% in mesentery). HCR-FISH for KI67 and BrdU labeling confirmed proliferating cells in the coelomic epithelium of the anlage.
results.evaluation: While reviewers accept the identification of a proliferating cluster, one reviewer explicitly notes 'There is no validation of the trajectory analysis and there is no validation of the proliferating cluster with H3P or EdU co-labeling.' The BrdU data is cited from previous work rather than being new validation, and the KI67 HCR-FISH is mentioned but its quality relative to standard proliferation markers is questioned.

results.result: C5 represents differentiating muscle precursor cells expressing muscle-specific markers (TITIN, MYL1, MYH7, ACTG, CNN3, TNNI1). HCR-FISH for MYH7 showed labeling in the basal region of the coelomic epithelium, and double labeling with muscle-specific antibodies confirmed co-expression in cells forming the actin-myosin contractile apparatus.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the muscle precursor identification. The editor notes 'high-quality RNA localization images' and one reviewer acknowledges 'Marker genes for cell types provided to the field.' The double labeling experiment provides strong validation of the muscle phenotype.

results.result: C9 represents neuroepithelial cells expressing neuronal genes (neurotrypsin, potassium channels, PRD10, ELAV2, STA10, beta-tubulin, synapsin). HCR-FISH for STA10 and double labeling with RN1 antibody showed cells in the coelomic epithelium forming fiber extensions typical of differentiating neurons.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the neuroepithelial cell identification. The HCR-FISH validation with double labeling is noted as providing good spatial context. One reviewer specifically mentions 'Identifying a proliferating cluster of cells is very interesting and may open avenues to identify the cell lineage history,' suggesting acceptance of differentiation pathways including neuronal.

results.result: C4 shows expression of genes like KCNQ5, SC6A9, EFNB2, and UNC5C, with GO enrichment for morphogenesis and sensory perception. Cells are predominantly from mesentery (67%) rather than anlage (37%). HCR-FISH for UNC5C showed intense labeling in normal intestine mesothelium and regenerating mesentery, suggesting C4 represents cells differentiating toward coelomic epithelia of the regenerated organ.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the characterization of C4, though the interpretation is acknowledged as more speculative. The HCR-FISH provides spatial validation, but the functional interpretation relies on gene expression patterns and trajectory analysis. One reviewer notes the spatial context 'is challenging to interpret in this spatially complex tissue organization.'

results.result: C0, C1, and C3 represent coelomic epithelial populations sharing developmental/regenerative genes and GO terms related to ribosomal activity. C1 and C3 are predominantly in the anlage (37% of anlage cells), while C0 is more associated with mesentery (27% of mesentery cells). HCR-FISH for NET1 (C1/C3 marker) and TRFM (C0 marker) showed differential spatial expression patterns, with NET1 high in anlage and TRFM high in normal intestine and showing a gradient in regenerating mesentery.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these as distinct coelomic epithelial populations. The HCR-FISH validation provides spatial context supporting the distinction between C0 and C1/C3. However, one reviewer notes 'The spatial context of the RNA localization images is challenging to interpret,' suggesting some difficulty in fully connecting the molecular data to tissue organization.

results.result: C1 and C3 are proposed as precursor cell populations of the anlage, expressing pluripotency-associated genes (HSP90A, HES1, TGFb, PIWL1, YAP1) and developmental transcription factors (Hox, zinc fingers). These cells appear capable of differentiating into muscle, neurons, coelomic epithelia, and mesenchymal cells. Trajectory analysis suggests C1 gives rise to C3 and represents the least differentiated state.
results.evaluation: Reviewers express mixed views on the precursor cell claims. While they acknowledge 'Interesting predictions about possible lineage relationships,' one reviewer explicitly states 'The conclusions of this paper are supported only by bioinformatic analyses' and 'There is no validation of the trajectory analysis.' Another reviewer notes the authors 'have done a good job in the revision of making sure not to overstate the lineage claims in absence of definitive lineage-tracing experiments,' indicating previous concerns about overinterpretation.

results.result: The coelomic epithelium of the anlage is proposed to be pluripotent tissue giving rise to diverse cell types of the regenerating intestine. This is supported by identification of multiple differentiation pathways and expression of pluripotency markers. The hypothesis is consistent with previous microscopy studies in echinoderms showing coelomic epithelium can differentiate into muscle, neurons, mesenchymal cells, and possibly immune cells.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge this as an important hypothesis but express reservations about the strength of evidence. One reviewer notes the work 'provides some new findings about organ regeneration, as well as the origins of pluripotent cells,' but another states 'The conclusions of this paper are supported only by bioinformatic analyses since the in vivo validation through HCR is not sufficient to support them.' The lack of lineage tracing experiments is a key limitation noted by reviewers.

results.result: RNA velocity and Slingshot pseudotime analyses suggest developmental trajectories: C5, C9, and C4 are terminal differentiated states; C8 (proliferating cells) transitions to C1; C1 is the least differentiated state giving rise to C3 and C4; C0 is in a more specialized differentiation state. The analyses support C1 as the main precursor population.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly question the trajectory analysis validation. One reviewer states 'There is no validation of the trajectory analysis,' which is a significant concern for these claims. While the bioinformatic analyses are acknowledged as standard approaches, the biological interpretation of trajectories as actual developmental relationships is not independently validated. The editor notes these are 'predictions about possible lineage relationships' rather than demonstrated lineages.

results.result: Immunocytochemical characterization of dissociated cells showed expected populations: 5% spherulocytes, 2-7% muscle (phalloidin+), 40% mesenchymal (KL14+), 32-60% mesothelial (MESO+), and 5-10% neurons in mesentery. Tubulin antibodies labeled 7-80% of cells depending on the antibody. Mature muscle cells and most neurons from the mesentery were not dissociated by the protocol.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this characterization as validation of the cell populations present in the samples. However, one reviewer notes 'The Authors frequently report the percentage of cells with a specific feature...This number can be misleading since that is calculated after cell dissociation and additional procedures...that can heavily bias the ratio between cell types.' This suggests the quantitative percentages should be interpreted cautiously, though the presence of these cell types is accepted.

results.result: The intestinal anlage is proposed to function as a blastema-like structure, with cells of the coelomic epithelium analogous to blastemal cells. Like amphibian blastemas, the anlage contains proliferating undifferentiated cells from dedifferentiation and expresses similar growth factors (Wnt, TGF-beta, FGF). However, unlike classical blastemas, cells with both blastema and apical epithelial cap (AEC) characteristics are found within the same coelomic epithelium layer, and both PRRX1 (blastema marker) and HES1 (AEC marker) are co-expressed.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the comparison to blastemas with appropriate caveats. One reviewer notes the authors 'have done a good job in the revision of making sure not to overstate' claims and suggests the terminology could be refined to say the anlage 'behaves like a blastema' rather than 'is a blastema.' The reviewer acknowledges 'there is ambiguity about the meaning of this term in the field' and appreciates the authors engaging with how blastema function may be more dispersed than traditionally appreciated. The comparison is accepted as conceptually useful while recognizing structural differences.

results.result: The lack of significant differences in cell clusters between anlage and mesentery is explained by: (1) cellular processes occur in a gradient extending from the anlage into the mesentery, and (2) mature muscle and neurons that would distinguish mesentery were not dissociated by the protocol.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these explanations for the observed similarity between anlage and mesentery samples. The gradient of regenerative processes is supported by previous citations. The technical limitation regarding muscle and neuron dissociation is acknowledged as a methodological constraint that affects interpretation but does not invalidate the findings.

comparisons.comparison: Both support the methodological approach and novelty (C3, C36, C37, C38, C41, C143). OpenEval emphasizes technical validation and quality control metrics, while peer reviewers highlight this as 'the first fundamental step to an unbiased approach' and acknowledge it as novel and valuable for the field.

Both support the clustering analysis and quantitative characterization (C57, C58, C59, C60, C61). OpenEval focuses on statistical validation, while peer reviewers note 'standard analyses providing well digested information' but also mention 'The Authors did not validate all the clusters,' indicating some reservations about complete validation.

Both support the broad characterization of cell types including epithelial and mesenchymal populations (C5, C6, C63-C73). OpenEval provides detailed validation through HCR-FISH and marker genes, while peer reviewers acknowledge the identification of cell clusters and their potential identities based on standard bioinformatic analyses.

Perfect agreement on coelomocyte identification (C78-C86, C152-C154). Both support the characterization based on immune-related gene expression and HCR-FISH validation. OpenEval notes this as the first expression profile in adult echinoderms, and peer reviewers accept the identification with 'convincing RNA localization images,' though note not all clusters were equally validated.

Both support mesenchymal cell characterization (C89-C95, C148-C151). OpenEval emphasizes ECM-related gene expression and pseudotime analysis supporting developmental relationships, while peer reviewers accept the characterization but note the EMT interpretation is 'supported only by bioinformatic analyses' without independent validation.

Divergent evaluations of proliferative cluster (C98-C102, C155). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED with strong evidence from proliferation markers, HCR-FISH, and BrdU labeling, while peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, explicitly noting 'There is no validation of the trajectory analysis and there is no validation of the proliferating cluster with H3P or EdU co-labeling.'

Perfect agreement on muscle precursor identification (C103-C107, C158-C159). Both strongly support the characterization based on muscle-specific markers, HCR-FISH spatial validation, and double labeling showing contractile apparatus formation. Peer reviewers note 'high-quality RNA localization images' and acknowledge marker genes provided to the field.

Perfect agreement on neuroepithelial cell identification (C108-C112, C160-C161). Both support the characterization based on neuronal markers, HCR-FISH validation, and double labeling. Peer reviewers specifically mention interest in the proliferating cluster opening avenues to identify cell lineage history, suggesting acceptance of neuronal differentiation pathways.

Both support C4 characterization as advanced developmental stage cells (C113-C118). OpenEval emphasizes GO enrichment and spatial distribution, while peer reviewers accept the characterization but note 'The spatial context of the RNA localization images is challenging to interpret' in this complex tissue organization.

Both support the identification of distinct coelomic epithelial populations C0, C1, and C3 (C119-C129, C163). OpenEval emphasizes differential gene expression and HCR-FISH validation, while peer reviewers accept the distinction but note challenges in interpreting spatial context in the complex tissue organization.

Both rate as UNCERTAIN regarding epithelial precursor cells and pluripotency claims (C9, C131-C133, C165-C166, C181). OpenEval notes evidence is consistent with pluripotency but lacks lineage tracing, while peer reviewers state 'conclusions are supported only by bioinformatic analyses' and note authors 'have done a good job not to overstate the lineage claims in absence of definitive lineage-tracing experiments.'

Both rate as UNCERTAIN regarding pluripotency claims (C10, C173-C177). OpenEval acknowledges the hypothesis is reasonable but requires additional validation, while peer reviewers note the work provides findings about 'origins of pluripotent cells' but state 'conclusions are supported only by bioinformatic analyses since the in vivo validation through HCR is not sufficient to support them.'

Divergent evaluations of trajectory analysis (C134-C142). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED, acknowledging appropriate computational methods with consistent results but noting inherent limitations, while peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, explicitly stating 'There is no validation of the trajectory analysis' and emphasizing these are 'predictions about possible lineage relationships' rather than demonstrated lineages.

Perfect agreement on blastema comparison (C182-C201). Both support the comparison with appropriate caveats. OpenEval notes this is primarily conceptual analysis based on gene expression similarities, while peer reviewers accept the comparison as conceptually useful, noting authors 'have done a good job not to overstate' claims and suggesting the anlage 'behaves like a blastema' while recognizing structural differences.

Perfect agreement on immunocytochemical characterization (C42-C54). Both support this as important validation of cell populations present in samples. OpenEval emphasizes quality control strengthening confidence in scRNA-seq results, while peer reviewers accept the characterization but caution that quantitative percentages 'can be misleading' due to dissociation procedures that may bias cell type ratios.

Both support the explanations for similarity between anlage and mesentery samples (C145-C147). OpenEval notes appropriate contextualization of study scope and limitations, while peer reviewers accept the biological gradient explanation and acknowledge technical limitations regarding muscle and neuron dissociation as methodological constraints.

Both rate as UNCERTAIN regarding SAA1 expression and coelomocyte generation hypothesis (C178-C180). OpenEval notes the observation is data-supported but the hypothesis remains speculative, appropriately presented as possibility rather than conclusion. Peer reviewers' UNCERTAIN rating for pluripotency claims encompasses related speculative hypotheses about cell origins.
